displayQuote: A man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone

meta.title: Who really said "A man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: Thoreau wrote it in Walden (1854), chapter 2, page 89 of the first edition — as a clause beginning "for a man is rich…". Source and scans here.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Thoreau. Traced to Walden, ch. 2, p. 89 of the 1854 Ticknor and Fields first edition — where it ends a sentence about leaving a farm fallow.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to the page. The words appear in Walden; or, Life in the Woods (Boston: Ticknor and Fields, 1854), chapter 2, “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For,” on page 89 of the first edition. Thoreau wrote it as the closing clause of a longer sentence — his own text runs “…and then I let it lie, fallow perchance, for a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone.”

source.heading: The passage in Walden

docMeta.dd: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
Chapter 2, “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For” — first paragraph, p. 89
Written in English — no translation involved

source.excerpt: An afternoon sufficed to lay out the land into orchard, woodlot, and pasture, and to decide what fine oaks or pines should be left to stand before the door, and whence each blasted tree could be seen to the best advantage; and then I let it lie, fallow perchance, for a man is rich in proportion to the number of things which he can afford to let alone.
trail: Searched the scanned text of the 1854 Ticknor and Fields first edition at the Internet Archive ↗ (Boston Public Library’s Rare Books copy). The sentence appears on p. 89, under the running head “WHERE I LIVED.”
Cross-checked the paragraph at Digital Thoreau ↗, whose fluid-text edition carries the identical wording in paragraph 1 of chapter 2.
Confirmed the same sentence in Project Gutenberg eBook #205 ↗, Walden, and On The Duty Of Civil Disobedience.
Checked the specialist reference: Wikiquote’s sourced Walden page ↗ lists the line under Chapter 2, “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For” — matching the first edition.
source.excerptNote: The familiar quotation begins mid-sentence. Thoreau’s clause opens with a lower-case “for”; popular versions capitalise the “A” and cut the farm loose from its reason.

source.rightsNote: Walden; or, Life in the Woods was first published in Boston by Ticknor and Fields on 9 August 1854, so the work — and this sentence with it — has long been in the public domain in the United States. Thoreau wrote in English, so there is no translation whose own copyright could still apply.

author.name: Henry David Thoreau
author.heading: Who was Henry David Thoreau?
author.bio: Henry David Thoreau was an American naturalist, essayist, poet and philosopher, born in Concord, Massachusetts on 12 July 1817 and dead at 44 on 6 May 1862. He is best known for Walden, his account of simple living beside Walden Pond, and for the essay “Civil Disobedience” (first published as “Resistance to Civil Government”). He lived at the pond from 4 July 1845 to 6 September 1847; Walden itself did not reach print until Ticknor and Fields published it on 9 August 1854.

misattribution.heading: What goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution itself is solid — no rival claimant, no fabrication, no ghost citation. What travels badly is the wording and the citation: the line is routinely trimmed, stripped of its source, and read as a standalone motto rather than as the reason clause Thoreau actually wrote.

items.who: The trimmed variant — “the number of things he can afford to let alone”
items.why: Thoreau wrote “things which he can afford to let alone.” The dropped relative pronoun is everywhere, including on BrainyQuote ↗ and on the Walden Woods Project’s own quotation index ↗, which prints the short form. The full-word version on Goodreads ↗ matches the 1854 text.

items.who: “Henry David Thoreau” with no work at all
items.why: BrainyQuote ↗ gives the line no book, chapter or page — only Thoreau’s dates. Goodreads ↗ names Walden but stops there. The chapter is nameable: Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗ places it in Chapter 2, “Where I Lived, and What I Lived For.”

items.who: The line read as a free-standing minimalism proverb
items.why: In Thoreau’s text it is not a maxim but a justification, hinging on a lower-case “for”: he lays out an imagined farm, leaves it fallow, and explains why. The full sentence is readable at Digital Thoreau ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Thoreau really wrote it, in these words. The sentence sits on page 89 of the 1854 Ticknor and Fields first edition, which you can turn page by page in the Boston Public Library’s scanned copy ↗.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: The line is the punchline of a joke about property. In the opening paragraph of chapter 2, Thoreau describes having bought, in his imagination, every farm for a dozen miles around Concord — walking the fields, tasting the wild apples, talking husbandry with each owner, and then quietly withdrawing before any deed changed hands. He calls the habit qualification enough to be “regarded as a sort of real-estate broker by my friends.”

Having laid out one of these imaginary estates into orchard, woodlot and pasture in a single afternoon, he leaves it fallow — and gives his reason. The sentence is not a standalone maxim about minimalism; it is Thoreau explaining why the pleasure of an unbought farm beat the burden of a bought one. A few sentences later comes the real-world proof: he nearly bought the Hollowell place, the seller’s wife changed her mind, and Thoreau — by his own account holding ten cents in the world — let him keep the farm and the ten dollars offered to release him.
detailsBody: The chapter opens on page 88 of the 1854 first edition, immediately after the Carew verse that closes “Economy.” The sentence falls on page 89, under the running head “WHERE I LIVED.”

Note the grammar of the original: Thoreau’s clause begins with a lower-case “for.” Every popular rendering silently promotes the clause to a sentence and capitalises the “A” — a harmless edit, but it is the reason the quotation reads as a proverb rather than as an argument.
